title: VSCD: Video-based Scene Change Detection in Unaligned Scenes
claim: Prior change-detection datasets assume similar viewpoints or simple trajectories; ours has unconstrained camera motion and strong misalignment between reference and query.
layout: 4 stacked rows of film strips, trajectory diagrams at right, legend bottom-right
description: The figure compares change detection datasets in stacked horizontal bands. Each band has a Reference row and a Query-plus-ground-truth row of frames, with magenta masks marking changed objects. The top band shows previous image-based data: street scenes in single frames, with a trajectory box showing nearly overlapping reference and query cameras. The second band shows previous video-based data: film strips of industrial pipes, with a straight back-and-forth arrow trajectory. The third band shows the proposed dataset: synthetic indoor rooms in film strips, with tangled, curved, non-overlapping red and green trajectories. The fourth band shows real-world dark bedroom frames and a query row with magenta clothing and object masks. A bottom-right legend explains the colors: magenta is ground truth, red is the reference camera and trajectory, and green is the query camera and trajectory. The eye goes first to the magenta masks and the contrast between the simple and tangled trajectory diagrams.
caption: Comparison between existing change detection datasets and our VSCD benchmark. Unlike prior image-based and video-based datasets that assume similar viewpoints or trajectories, VSCD features unconstrained camera motion, which leads to strong misalignment between reference and query videos.
abstract: Detecting what has changed in an environment is essential for long-term autonomy, yet most change detection settings assume fixed viewpoints, mild misalignment, or only a few changed objects. We introduce Video-based Scene Change Detection (VSCD), which predicts a pixel-wise change mask for each query frame, given a reference and a query RGB video of the same indoor space recorded at different times under unconstrained camera motion. The two videos are not temporally synchronized, and many object instances may appear or disappear. To study this setting, we build a large-scale benchmark with over 1.1 million frames annotated with pixel-accurate change masks, together with a real-world test set for evaluating transfer beyond simulation. We propose a query-centric multi-reference model that learns temporal matching implicitly from change-mask supervision, aligns candidate reference features to the query via local patch correspondence, and fuses per-candidate change features using frame-level and patch-level confidence before decoding a high-resolution mask once per frame. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance against strong image- and video-based baselines, and we validate its real-world impact by deploying it on a mobile robot for two downstream applications -- visual surveillance and object incremental learning.
